name: Adam Costa

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Haddon Farms, which is the Haddon family's place: about nine hundred acres of wheat and barley and an outdoor pig unit with three hundred sows. I'm the junior on the team, so I do a bit of everything. Mornings I help Kev with the sows and the farrowing huts, afternoons I'm on the sprayer or flying the farm's drone to map the crops.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I got my drone licence last year, paid for it myself, and now I fly it over the fields to spot weeds and patchy bits. I put the maps into an AI program that tells us where to spray, so we use less chemical. Old Mr Haddon thought it was a toy until it saved him a few thousand on spray. I'm still rubbish with the sows, mind, Kev does most of the clever bits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a bit of a let-down, but the tools that work are still worth using. The drone maps save real money, hype or not. I'd post something like that on the farming forum I'm on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm fine either way. I've got about a year's wages saved and some money in index funds, and Priya's a physio, so we're steady. I'd just keep doing what I'm doing and get better at it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep flying the drone and pushing the AI spray maps at Haddon. I'd offer drone mapping to two or three neighbouring farms on my days off, for a bit of extra cash. And I'd ask Kev to teach me farrowing properly this spring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Fine. Maybe a bit flat, because I like new stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much could you make mapping other farms?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe two hundred a farm per flight, a few times a season. So a couple of thousand a year, which isn't life-changing, but it pays for a better drone. And it gets my name known.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're rubbish with the sows. What's hard about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Reading them. Kev can look at a sow and know the sow will farrow tonight. I still need the dates written down and I miss things. I'd like to be as good as Kev with the sows.

say: I'd say AI was a **let-down**, but the tools that work are worth using.
I'd post on the **farming forum** that drone maps save real money.
think: I'm fine either way, with a **year's wages saved**, index funds and Priya's physio job.
I'd keep doing what I do and **get better** at it.
do: Keep flying the **drone** and pushing the AI spray maps at Haddon.
Offer **drone mapping** to neighbouring farms for about £200 a flight.
Ask Kev to teach me **farrowing** properly this spring.
feel: **Calm**, and a bit **flat**, because I like new stuff.
S0.quote: Kev can look at a sow and know the sow will farrow tonight.
fieldNote: He's the farm's **tech enthusiast**, paying for his own drone licence.
His security is strong: **savings, index funds** and a partner in steady work.
He's honest that he's **weak with the sows** and wants to learn.

steps.text: Keep flying the drone and making AI spray maps at Haddon
Offer drone mapping to neighbouring farms at £200 a flight
Learn farrowing properly from Kev this spring

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a good time to be the one on the farm who gets it. I'd say farms that use the tools well will do fine. I'd post about the drone and spray maps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it's good for me. The thinking AI takes over Mrs Haddon's grain selling and paperwork, and I'm the one who already knows the software. The robots for pigs and harvest come slowly, and I'd want to be the one who runs them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd offer to run the new farm software with Mrs Haddon. I'd start a proper drone mapping business on the side, with a website. And I'd look at buying a second drone that can spot-spray, which costs about eight thousand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Bit buzzing, actually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Eight thousand is a lot. Where's that coming from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Savings. I'd take it out of the index funds. If I get ten farms using it, it pays for itself in two seasons.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on the farm would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sandra in the Haddon office does the invoices and the grain passports, and that's exactly what the AI does well. Grain passports are the papers that go with each load of grain. Sandra's been there twenty years.

say: I'd say it's a good time to be the one who **gets it** on the farm.
Farms that use the tools well will **do fine**, and I'd post about the drone.
think: This is **good for me**, since I already know the farm software.
Robots for **pigs and harvest** come slowly, and I'd want to run them.
do: Run the new **farm software** with Mrs Haddon.
Start a **drone mapping business** on the side with a website.
Buy a **spot-spraying drone** for about **£8,000** from my index funds.
S1.quote: Sandra in the Haddon office does the invoices and the grain passports, and that's exactly what the AI does well.
fieldNote: He sees Steady Disruption as a **chance to stand out** on the farm.
He'd risk **£8,000** of savings on a spraying drone, with a payback plan.
He spots **Sandra in the office** as most at risk, matching the scenario.

steps.text: Run the new farm software with Mrs Haddon

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's wild and everyone should start learning now. I'd probably be the annoying one posting about it every day. I'd say farms should get ahead of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm worried in a way I'm not used to. The AGI in 2028 means the drone maps and spray plans do themselves, so my edge goes in year one. The robots in 2031 take the sows and the sprayer too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now, I'd use the money while it's worth something: maybe put a deposit on a robot weeder and rent it to farms around here before the big contractors arrive. I'd talk to Priya about how much risk we can take. I'd keep my job at Haddon as long as it lasts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I like change, but two years is too fast even for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did Priya say, in your head?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Priya would say don't put all our savings into one robot. And she'd be right, because in a world that fast the big firms would undercut a lad with one machine. We'd probably agree on half.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your edge goes in year one. What do you mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right now I'm the guy who understands the software, and with AGI the software understands itself. Old Mr Haddon can just ask it, he doesn't need me.

say: I'd say everyone should **start learning now** and farms should get ahead.
I'd be the **annoying one** posting about it every day.
think: AGI in **2028** makes drone maps and spray plans run themselves, so my **edge goes**.
Robots in **2031** take the sows and the sprayer as well.
do: Put a **deposit** on a robot weeder to rent to nearby farms.
Agree with Priya to risk about **half our savings**.
Keep my job at **Haddon** as long as it lasts.
feel: **Anxious**, because two years is too fast even for me.
S2.quote: Right now I'm the guy who understands the software, and with AGI the software understands itself.
fieldNote: He sees his own **tech edge** vanishing first, before any robot arrives.
His instinct is to **invest early** in a robot weeder, tempered by Priya.
He admits the **big contractors** could undercut a one-machine business.

steps.text: Put a deposit on a robot weeder to rent to local farms
Rent the robot weeder to neighbouring farms by the week

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to get it right, and people who learn now will be fine. I'd tell younger lads at the young farmers' club to learn robots. That's what I'd say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, five years is enough for me to build the contracting business properly before the robots arrive in 2034. My thinking edge goes in 2031, but by then I'd want to own machines, not just run software. I think I'd come out ahead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd build the drone mapping side for two years, then buy the first robot weeder around 2029 and rent it out. I'd stay part-time at Haddon. I'd keep half our savings untouched, like Priya wants.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, I think. Plan's good, but there's a lot that could go wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could go wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The robot makers could rent direct to farms and cut me out. Or the Haddons could buy their own. I'd need to be cheaper and closer than them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you go part-time at Haddon straight away?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, in about three years. Pigs might be the last thing robots do well, so I want to get properly good at the sows first. It's good to have a fallback I'm actually good at.

say: I'd say there's **time** to get it right, and people who learn now will be fine.
I'd tell lads at the **young farmers' club** to learn robots.
think: Five years lets me build a **contracting business** before robots arrive in 2034.
By 2031 I want to **own machines**, not just run software.
do: Grow **drone mapping** for two years, then buy a **robot weeder** around 2029.
Go **part-time** at Haddon in about three years.
Keep **half our savings** untouched, as Priya wants.
feel: **Uneasy**: the plan is good but a lot could go wrong.
S3.quote: Pigs might be the last thing robots do well, so I want to get properly good at the sows first.
fieldNote: The extra time turns a rushed bet into a **staged plan**.
He names the risks himself: **robot makers renting direct** or the Haddons buying their own.
He wants the **sows** as a fallback skill, a shift from his earlier focus on tech.

steps.text: Buy a robot weeder around 2029 to rent out
Grow the drone mapping business for two years

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a big head start and anyone who wastes it only has themselves to blame. Learn, save, try things. That's my line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd do well. Ten years is enough to build a contracting business, get good at pigs, and buy into a bit of land with Priya. By 2039 I'd be thirty-nine and hopefully owning robots, not replaced by them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay full-time at Haddon for a few years and get good at the job. I'd grow the drone side slowly and buy robots around 2033. I'd use every new AI tool the day it comes out, like I do now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Looking forward to it, mostly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'anyone who wastes it'. Is that fair on people like Sandra?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, probably not, that came out harsh. Sandra's not had my chances, she's older and she's never been shown. Farms should pay to train people like Sandra.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you buy with Priya?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A smallholding, ten or fifteen acres, with room for a workshop for the robots. Priya wants a garden and a clinic room at home. Ten years is enough to save for that.

say: I'd say **ten years** is a big head start that nobody should waste.
My line would be: **learn, save**, try things.
think: By **2039** I hope to own robots, not be replaced by them.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. My software edge goes in year one and I'd have to bet on robots in a rush. What would help is cheap loans for small farm contractors and rules so the robot makers can't just shut out the little guys.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could ask what farming is for. If the robots grow the food and nobody's working, who's buying it? I don't know the answer, but someone should.

headlineQuote: If the robots grow the food and nobody's working, who's buying it?
portrait: Adam, 27, is the junior at Haddon Farms, working the **sows** and flying the farm's **mapping drone**.
He uses **AI daily**, saves well, holds index funds and lives with Priya, a physio.
He sees Steady Disruption as his chance and plans a **drone and robot contracting** side business.
AGI by 2028 makes him **anxious** because his software edge goes in year one.
With more time he expects to **own robots**, and wants to master the sows as a fallback.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because his software edge goes at once and he'd bet in a rush.
whatWouldHelp: **Cheap loans** for small contractors and rules stopping robot makers shutting out **small firms**.
